title: CPU-side bottlenecks: threadpool & request parsing experiments
content:
Summary:

This working doc captures a set of profiling experiments focused on CPU-side bottlenecks we’ve observed in the serving runtime: tokenization, request parsing (JSON validation + schema checks), thread-pool sizing/behavior, and general Python overhead (GIL/dispatch). The goal is to surface root causes for observed P95/P99 latency spikes and propose low-effort mitigations plus next steps for production rollouts.

Context / Motivation:
- Customer reports + internal benchmarks show tail latency regressions for short requests (few tokens). Baseline p50/p95/p99 and CPU profile attach to RINF-2345.
- Typical host used for tests: 8vCPU (Intel Xeon), 32GB RAM; serving runtime binary in docker image redwood/serving:canary-202510. Workload: 50 RPS steady, 1-8 token prompts (median 3).

Baseline measurements (before experiments):
- Baseline (canary-202510) on 8vCPU, 50 RPS: p50=28ms, p95=210ms, p99=430ms.
- CPU usage: steady ~72% across cores, spikes to 95% during tail events.
- Per-request CPU breakdown (sampled via eBPF + perf): tokenization ~45% of CPU cycles, request parsing (JSON decode + validation) ~18%, Python dispatch & marshalling ~15%, threadpool/locking/idle overhead ~10%, other (I/O, logging) ~12%.

Profiling methodology:
- flamegraphs collected with py-spy on live container for 30m windows (heatmap + stack samples).
- eBPF (bcc) used to attribute kernel-time vs user-time and syscall hotspots.
- microbenchmarks for tokenizers: measured both Python tokenizer (pure-CPython split logic) and Rust-based fast-tokenizer binding compiled as a Python wheel.
- JSON parsing profiled with cProfile and sampling; compared json.loads (stdlib) vs orjson.

Key findings / observations:
1) Tokenization dominates short-request CPU: ~30-40ms per request on average for current Python tokenizer implementation. This is primarily due to per-request object allocation + Python-level loops. Flamegraph shows repeated calls into tokenizer.tokenize and large proportion of time in pure Python loops.

2) Request parsing has disproportionate impact on tail: stdlib json.loads + schema validation (pydantic-like) accounts for ~12ms median and large variance (up to 80ms on tails) because of repeated exception handling and deep nested validation logic.

3) Threadpool sizing & contention: we use a ThreadPoolExecutor with a default max_workers tuned to CPU cores. Under bursty traffic the pool saturates and request-handling threads contend for a small critical section (KV cache lock + metrics aggregator). This creates queueing and long waits observed in kernel stacks.

4) Python overhead (GIL + context switches): while not the largest single consumer, GIL contention appears exacerbated by expensive Python tokenization and blocking I/O calls. Heavy Python functions hold the GIL for tens of ms, blocking other threads and increasing tail latency.

Experiments run and results:
A) Replace Python tokenizer with Rust fast-tokenizer (pyO3 binding)
- Setup: pip wheel of tokenizer-rust v0.3, replace tokenizer imports, keep same tokenization config.
- Result: tokenization latency dropped from ~35ms -> ~5ms (median); total request p95 reduced ~60% (210ms -> 85ms), p99 reduced ~45% (430ms -> 235ms). CPU utilization decreased ~18 percentage points.
- Notes: minimal code changes in runtime; binary size + native dependency in container increased image by ~6MB. No functional diffs observed on token outputs for our canonical models.

B) Switch JSON parsing path to orjson + simpler validation layer
- Setup: replace json.loads with orjson.loads, replace pydantic full validation for thin-schema check (manual lightweight checks in C-extension friendly code paths).
- Result: parsing median 12ms -> 2ms; tail variance reduced significantly. Total p95 dropped further (~85ms -> ~70ms) in combination with tokenizer change.

C) Move expensive validation off critical path (async pre-check)
- Idea: accept payload, enqueue heavy schema checks to background worker; return 202 if validation pending for non-critical fields or run permissive path for opentelemetry-style headers.
- Result: reduces blocking on main thread for certain requests, but increases complexity; observed fewer p99 spikes for short-path requests. Trade-offs documented in confluence doc.

D) Threadpool sizing and lock profiling
- Experimented with increasing ThreadPoolExecutor max_workers from default(=os.cpu_count()*5) -> 4x. Observed improved throughput but only up to a point: kernel scheduling overhead and GIL contention caused diminishing returns and memory pressure.
- Found a single lock (kv_cache.py:Line ~142) serializing access for cache insertions; this was the main queuing point seen in kernel stacks.
- Replacing the global lock with a sharded lock (16 shards hashed by prefix) reduced wait times and improved p99 by ~30ms under load.

E) Async path and uvloop
- Ported request parsing + tokenization orchestration to asyncio + uvloop for an experiment. Results: slightly improved median latency but no consistent p99 improvement because tokenization still held the GIL in Python implementation. Combined with Rust tokenizer this path performed best for throughput-limited tests.

Actionable recommendations (prioritized):
1) Ship Rust-based tokenizer replacement (low risk, high impact). Owner: Marcus Patel. Target: experimental rollout on canary pool in 2 sprints.
2) Replace stdlib json.loads with orjson in hot-paths + move to lightweight validation for request body. Owner: Lena Ortiz. Target: canary next week (small PR).
3) Shard the KV cache lock to remove global contention. Owner: Oliver Reed. Target: next sprint.
4) Add a pre-tokenization cache for identical prefixes we see commonly in short prompts (LRU with small memory cap). Owner: Samira Gupta. Target: spike this week; can be rolled as opt-in config flag.
5) Long-term: expose a C-extension or native pre-processor for critical parsing/validation used by enterprise customers (private deployments). Track feasibility in RINF-2390.

Low-risk quick wins (immediate):
- Bake orjson into image and flip flag for parsing (canary-only first).
- Increase ThreadPoolExecutor sizing in staging for high-concurrency scenarios while monitoring memory.
- Add flamegraph collection to canary nightly runs and a perf-dash board to track tokenization/parse times by route.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Token equivalence: need broader regression tests for tokenizer differences across languages (JP/KR) and model tokenization edge cases.
- Memory impact for Rust tokenizer on many concurrent requests; need soak test for 24h at 200 RPS.
- For private/on-prem installs where native wheels are harder, need a pure-Python fallback path; consider shipping prebuilt wheels for common platforms.

Next steps / owners & dates:
- Marcus: prepare PR for rust-tokenizer integration + canonical tokenization test suite (due 2026-03-10).
- Lena: flip orjson on canary and measure delta in nightly runs; share metrics in #eng-serving-runtime (due 2026-02-28).
- Oliver: implement sharded-kv-lock prototype and benchmark (due 2026-03-17).
- Samira: spike pre-tokenization cache and run 24h soak at 200 RPS (due 2026-03-05).

Notes / references:
- Flamegraphs + perf traces uploaded to Confluence page (see linked artifacts).
- PR with tokenizer changes: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/842
- Jira epic: JIRA-RINF-2345 (CPU-side perf: tokenization + parsing)

This doc is a working record; expect follow-ups and iteration. Feedback welcome - add comments inline or ping on Slack thread linked in metadata.
